I’m responding as someone living in England in my late twenties who wants a fair, workable path to better private renting. In practice, that means a bigger, better-quality supply of affordable homes, backed by stronger standards and sensible regulation that doesn’t push decent landlords out of the market. I think the most effective route is a package that combines planning reform and incentives to grow supply (especially on brownfield sites and through build-to-rent and social housing expansion) with mandatory, practical improvements in how the private rental sector is managed and regulated.

First, expand supply through planning reform and targeted incentives. Brownfield development should be the default starting point, with local authorities required to publish and actively promote brownfield registers and streamline consent processes for credible schemes. If we can halve the time it takes to approve well-located conversions or new flats on derelict sites, we’ll see more affordable homes on the ground without sprawling greenfield estates.

Build-to-rent can play a major part, but only if it’s designed with tenants in mind. Long, well-managed tenancies, high-energy standards, and transparent pricing should be built in from the start. Governments could offer incentives such as tax relief or accelerated depreciation for BTR schemes that deliver a defined share of genuinely affordable units or cross-subsidise good-quality rents in the long term. Importantly, infrastructure and services — schools, healthcare, and transport links — must be planned in parallel with delivery, not tacked on after a development opens. In my area, new flats looked attractive, but the road network and GP capacity lagged behind, making daily life more stressful and expensive. A funded, phased approach that guarantees service readiness in early phases would prevent communities from being born into bottlenecks.

Social housing expansion should be scaled up, with councils and housing associations driving schemes on brownfield sites and in areas of high demand. Viability tests need to be fair and transparent, so genuinely affordable homes aren’t delayed or diluted. S106 and CIL should deliver real local benefits, with clear delivery milestones and public reporting so residents can see the outcomes rather than vague promises.

Second, raise standards across the sector through compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing, and mandatory training. A national register for landlords and letting agents, with compulsory renewals and penalties for non-compliance, would create a baseline of competence. Mandatory licensing should include minimum safety and quality standards (gas and electrical safety, damp and insulation, heating efficiency, timely repairs) and clear expectations on tenancy management and tenant rights. Accreditation and ongoing training would be tied to professional development, so agents and landlords keep up with best practice and legal changes.

I know from lived experience that some properties fall short on safety and comfort, often because tenants don’t have the right channels to report issues or because managers aren’t accountable. A robust registration system would also make it easier for tenants to check who they’re dealing with and for councils to target enforcement where it’s most needed. There should be exemptions or phased entry for very small landlords, but with a clear plan to bring them into compliance over time. Enforcement must be funded and proportionate; penalties should be used to fund further enforcement and to remedy harms, not simply to raise fines.

Third, link security, affordability and standards through tenancy and rent-affordability safeguards. Longer tenancies with predictable, affordable rent reviews help families budget and stay stable, while still allowing reasonable adjustments for inflation and wage growth. For landlords, there must be a fair framework that recognises upgrades and compliance costs; grants or low-interest loans could support energy efficiency improvements and safety upgrades without breaking viability.

Finally, ensure the reforms don’t inadvertently shrink supply. Clear exemptions or graduated requirements for the smallest landlords, and a credible enforcement regime funded by the sector itself, will help avoid pushing decent landlords out. Regular reporting on delivery rates, rental trends, energy efficiency, and service standards should be public so communities can hold systems to account.

In short, I want a housing market where more genuinely affordable homes are built, where tenants can feel secure in well-managed, safe homes, and where landlords who meet clear standards can operate with confidence. A coordinated package of planning reform, incentives for build-to-rent and social housing, plus compulsory licensing and training for landlords and agents, offers the best chance to achieve that balance and sustain a healthy rental market for the long term.

Security and tenure

Accessibility, discrimination and tailored support
- Strengthen anti-discrimination measures and require reasonable adaptations. People with disabilities, older tenants, BAME communities, young adults and others deserve a housing system that treats them fairly and makes practical changes feasible. Affordability and supply through planning and investment

Local experience and impact

Expanding tenancy security, improving accessibility, and boosting affordable supply would help families stay put, while ensuring the market remains viable for landlords who maintain well-managed properties.

It would protect vulnerable renters, support workers and families, and create more stable communities without undermining landlord viability or the incentives to invest in quality homes.

Strengthened grounds and fair, timely processes will improve tenant security and reduce escalations that harm communities.
